newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - TI says on target for further growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - TI says on target for further growth.

text.p: International engineering firm TI Group Plc unveiled a solid advance in profits on Wednesday and predicted further growth this year, despite difficult conditions in some European markets.
Pretax profits for 1996 were up 26 percent at 232.2 million pounds ($369 million) last year, with underlying profits before an exceptional gain from disposals up 16 percent at 211.1 million pounds.
Sales rose to 1.76 billion pounds from 1.70 billion in 1995, with underlying sales growth up eight percent after adjusting for acquisitions and disposals.

Chairman Sir Christopher Lewinton said the group was well positioned by region and product to make further progress in 1997. This was despite what he said would be "another challenging year, particularly in Europe...But I think it will be a successful year".

In particular the company said its Bundy division making specialist tubing had faced the brunt of the problems, which were in European automotive markets. But weakness in France and Sweden had been offset by increased output in Britain, Spain and Germany.

Overall the group expected to continue expanding through organic growth and further acquisitions, having widened its geographical spread last year thanks to accelerating growth in the Asia-Pacific region and Latin America.
The confident note was endorsed by investors and the share price closed up 12 pence at 576p, off the day's high of 584.

Several analysts said after a results meeting that they expected to raise their forecasts for the current year to around 240 million pounds pretax before any exceptionals, from current forecasts ranging between 210 and 235 million.
"These were boringly good results again," said one analyst. "It is a case of steady as she goes," said another.

The final dividend was increased a penny to 9.75 pence, making 14.5p for the year, up from 13.1p in 1995. Earnings per share were up 29 percent at 34.1p, and up 16 percent at 30 pence before the exceptional gains of 21.1 million pounds.
Analysts had forecast pre-tax profits of between 208 and 215 million pounds and a dividend of 14.3 pence.

The firm said it spent another 275 million pounds on more acquisitions last year to add to its core businesses of John Crane mechanical seals and engineering polymers, Bundy tubing, mainly for the automotive and refrigeration markets, and the Dowty aerospace business.
"We have had another very good year," said Lewinton.
"Our order books are healthy and our current trading is in line with expectations so all in all we are very pleased," he told Reuters in an interview.

"All our core businesses have grown in double-digit terms for many many years now and they are still not bumping their heads against the ceiling...TI in my view can keep doing this for many, many years."

Lewinton said TI would continue its policy of the last five years of steadily making acquisitions. "We have very good (interest) cover, we have low gearing and we have strong cash generation," he said.
After acquisitions TI had net debt of 68 million pounds at the end of 1996, to put gearing at 21 percent of net assets of 325 million pounds.

Operating activities generated cash of 229.7 million pounds from 224.7 million pounds in 1995 and net cash after capital expenditure, interest, tax and dividends of 51.8 million pounds. Interest cover rose to 43 times operating profits from 22 times in 1995.

Sales in North America rose to 750.8 million pounds from 680.3 million in 1995. Mainland European sales dipped to 536.2 million from 555 million pounds but sales in markets outside north America and Europe rose to 248.4 million pounds from 211.7 million in 1995.
British markets accounted for sales of 221.2 million pounds, down from 256.3 million a year ago.
TI said its Dowty aerospace components division was set for lift-off on the back of the current revival in fortunes for the aircraft industry.

Dowty chief Tony Edwards said there was a 29 percent growth in underlying operating profits on a nine percent rise in sales last year, reflecting airlines taking delivery of more new aircraft. "It's good to be out of recession at last," he told Reuters.
